title.en: Convert between binary and Gray code

say.en: A digital clock shows each digit separately, a rotary encoder must never misread a position, and a keyboard sends letters. Each job uses a different binary code. In this lesson: Write BCD and Excess-3 codes.
Convert between binary and Gray code.
Describe ASCII.

body.en: In BCD (8421 code) each decimal digit is written as its own 4-bit *binary* group; codes 1010 to 1111 are invalid. BCD is a weighted code (weights 8, 4, 2, 1). Excess-3 is obtained by adding 3 (0011) to each BCD digit; it is non-weighted and self-complementing (the 1's complement of a digit's code gives the code of its 9's complement).

narration.en: In B C D each decimal digit gets its own four bits. Excess-three adds three to each digit before coding.

title.en: On the board: BCD, Excess-3 and Gray

say.en: In BCD each decimal digit gets its own 4 bits. 47 becomes 0100 for the 4 and 0111 for the 7.
Excess-3: add 3, that is 0011, to each BCD digit. 4 becomes 0111 and 7 becomes 1010.
Gray code: copy the MSB, then each Gray bit is the XOR of two neighbouring binary bits. 1101 becomes 1011.
ASCII is a 7-bit code for letters, digits and symbols. Capital A is 65, which is 1000001.

body.en: In *Gray code* only one bit changes between successive numbers, so it avoids errors in shaft encoders. Binary → Gray: the MSB is copied, then each Gray bit is the XOR of adjacent binary bits. Gray → binary: copy the MSB, then each binary bit is the XOR of the previous binary bit and the next Gray bit. ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) is a 7-bit alphanumeric code; for example 'A' = 65 = 1000001.

narration.en: Gray code changes only one bit at a time, which is why it is used in position encoders. ASCII gives every letter and symbol a seven-bit code.

heading.en: BCD, Excess-3, Gray and ASCII Codes

tagline.en: Weighted and unweighted codes, BCD and BCD addition, the Excess-3 code, Gray code and conversions, ASCII, and parity bits for error detection.

myth.en: BCD of 59 is 111011, the binary of 59.

truth.en: BCD codes each decimal digit separately: 59 → 0101 1001. Straight binary of 59 is 111011. BCD is easier for displays (each digit drives its own 7-segment display) but uses more bits than binary, and it is not the same number written in base 2.

say.en: In Binary Coded Decimal, each decimal digit is written separately as a 4-bit binary number. So (59)₁₀ = 0101 1001 in BCD, while in straight binary 59 = 111011.
Excess-3 (XS-3) code of a decimal digit is its BCD code plus 3 (0011). So 5 → 0101 + 0011 = 1000, and 59 → 1000 1100.

ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) is a 7-bit alphanumeric code with 2⁷ = 128 characters: letters, digits, punctuation and control codes. 'A' is 65 (1000001), 'a' is 97 (1100001) and the digit '0' is 48 (0110000).

explain.en: BCD and XS-3 code decimal digits; Gray code is chosen for unit-distance changes; ASCII codes text; a parity bit checks for errors.

narration.en: Many people think: BCD of 59 is 111011, the binary of 59. Actually: BCD codes each decimal digit separately: 59 → 0101 1001. Straight binary of 59 is 111011. problem.en: Write (92)₁₀ in BCD and in Excess-3 code.

narration.en: Let us work this out together. Write (92)₁₀ in BCD and in Excess-3 code.

say.en: Let us work this out together. Write 92 10 in BCD and in Excess-3 code.
BCD: 9 equals 1001, 2 equals 0010 gives 1001 0010.
Excess-3: 9 plus 3 equals 12 equals 1100, 2 plus 3 equals 5 equals 0101 gives 1100 0101.
So the answer is BCD 1001 0010; Excess-3 1100 0101.

problem.en: Convert the binary number 1101 to Gray code, and the Gray code 1011 back to binary.

answer.en: Gray of 1101 is 1011, and Gray 1011 is binary 1101

narration.en: Let us work this out together. Convert the binary number 1101 to Gray code, and the Gray code 1011 back to binary.

say.en: Let us work this out together. Convert the binary number 1101 to Gray code, and the Gray code 1011 back to binary.
Binary gives Gray: copy 1; 1⊕1 equals 0; 1⊕0 equals 1; 0⊕1 equals 1 gives 1011.
Gray gives binary: copy 1; 1⊕0 equals 1; 1⊕1 equals 0; 0⊕1 equals 1 gives 1101.
So the answer is Gray of 1101 is 1011, and Gray 1011 is binary 1101.
